```{=html}
<p class="lx-hint">1 MWh of power makes 17.5 kg of hydrogen, which holds 0.58 MWh; a fuel cell turns that back into 0.35 MWh. Cost per kg counts capital and power only.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow" style="margin-top:1rem">Eight uses of hydrogen, sorted by their alternative today</p>
<table class="lx-facts a16-fb a16-uses">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Use</th><th scope="col">Where it sits</th><th scope="col">Why</th></tr></thead>

<tr><td>Oil refining</td><td data-label="Sits">Hydrogen is the feedstock</td><td data-label="Why">Refineries already use over 43 Mt a year (IEA, 2024): the choice is how it is made.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Steel from iron ore (direct reduction)</td><td data-label="Sits">Hydrogen is the feedstock</td><td data-label="Why">Hydrogen can replace the gas that strips oxygen from the ore; about 10% of industry's hydrogen today (IEA).</td></tr>
<tr><td>Fuel for ocean shipping</td><td data-label="Sits">Both routes are tried</td><td data-label="Why">Long voyages need dense fuels; ammonia and methanol made from hydrogen compete with others.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Power storage for weeks</td><td data-label="Sits">Both routes are tried</td><td data-label="Why">Salt caverns hold weeks of energy cheaply, but only about 31% comes back (A8).</td></tr>
<tr><td>Long-haul trucks</td><td data-label="Sits">Both routes are tried</td><td data-label="Why">Fuel cells and batteries are both tried; a battery truck uses far less electricity per mile.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Passenger cars</td><td data-label="Sits">Electricity does it with far less</td><td data-label="Why">Electric car: 100 miles on 25–40 kWh. Fuel cell car: about 60 miles per kg, made with 57 kWh: about 1 mile per kWh.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Heating homes</td><td data-label="Sits">Electricity does it with far less</td><td data-label="Why">A heat pump gives up to three times the heat of the power it uses; hydrogen loses about 40% before any heat is made.</td></tr>
</tbody>
```

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a16-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Energy balance</dt><dd>1 MWh makes 17.5 kg; it holds 0.58 MWh and gives back 0.35 MWh through a fuel cell.</dd>
<dt>Utilization</dt><dd>On spare wind a 20 MW electrolyzer's average utilization is 18%: it runs in 2,408 hours, at full size in 662. Each kg carries much capital: $4.24 per kg.</dd>
<dt>Part-load limit</dt><dd>At 20 MW an alkaline unit (15% minimum) loses 420 MWh of spare wind a year below its minimum; a PEM unit (5%) loses 47 MWh.</dd>
<dt>Cost per kg and the system</dt><dd>At $4 per kg the cheapest kg comes at 5 MW, the owner's best size at 10 MW.</dd>
<dt>Storage</dt><dd>Steady delivery of a 20 MW unit's 2025 output needs at least 88 t of working storage, 59 days of delivery, with 44 t in the tank on 1 January and no losses.</dd>
<dt>Matching rules</dt><dd>A rule sets what may be claimed; what is emitted depends on what the grid does in the hours bought.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>Slide the hydrogen price</h3></header>
<div class="explainer" data-explainer="wind-hydrogen">
<ol class="ex-fallback lx-ex-static"><li>A higher hydrogen price makes each kilogram worth more, so the optimizer builds a larger electrolyzer to capture more surplus wind.</li><li>The extra capacity runs fewer full-load hours, so the cost per kilogram, the levelized cost of hydrogen, goes up.</li><li>Yet the added hydrogen revenue lowers the net cost of the whole system.</li><li>The cost per kilogram and the system's cost move in opposite directions.</li></ol>
</div>
<p class="lx-hint">A separate example with stylized numbers, from the course author's open explainer: not the study's data or results.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">It has its own wind shape and costs, and reads out the whole system's net cost, so its sizes and dollars differ from this lesson's farm.</p>
</div>
<script src="../assets/explainers/common.js" defer></script>
<script src="../assets/explainers/wind-hydrogen.js" defer></script>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Colours, claims and matching rules</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Colours are names, not measurements.** Grey (natural gas), blue (gas with capture) and green (renewable electrolysis) are common labels; the IEA says it “does not use colours” and counts low-emissions hydrogen instead.
- **What rules measure.** DOE's clean-hydrogen target is at most 4.0 kg [CO₂e]{.lx-term term="co2e"} per kg, [well-to-gate]{.lx-term term="well-to-gate"}.
- **DOE's example.** A gas reformer with about 95% carbon capture could reach about 4.0, if it uses the average U.S. grid mix and upstream methane leaks stay at or below 1%.
- **Three tests of the power.** The U.S. clean-hydrogen credit's final rules (January 2025) ask for [deliverability]{.lx-term term="deliverability"} (the same region), temporal matching (the same year or the same hour) and incrementality (new clean power).
- **Matching is not accounting.** Matching sets which power may count. Separately, from 2030 DOE's 45VH2-GREET manual (December 2025) lets a producer opt to count its electricity's emissions hour by hour, if its annual result is at most 4.0 kg.
- **A claim is not a cause.** Matching sets what a buyer may claim. Whether emissions fall depends on whether the clean power is new ([additionality]{.lx-term term="additionality"}) and deliverable: the accounting questions of [A10](a10-emissions-questions.qmd).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>From rules to an optimization model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Here** each hour follows a rule: run at the spare wind, or stop below the minimum load. The size is chosen by trying sizes.
- **In a model** the solver chooses the size, the tank and every hour's operation at once.
- **The tank's balance:** $L_t = L_{t-1} + h_t - q_t$.
- **Its symbols:** $L_t$ is the hydrogen in the tank at the end of hour $t$, $h_t$ the hour's production and $q_t$ its delivery, all in kg.
- **A minimum load** is a yes-or-no choice per hour (on or off), so an exact model is a [mixed-integer program]{.lx-term term="mixed-integer-program"}; a linear program can only force the unit on or ignore the limit.
- **Next.** [M4](m04-storage-multienergy.html) builds such a plant model with a battery, a hydrogen tank and a heat store.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Upkeep and stack replacement, which DOE's $5–7 per kg production cost counts.</li>
<li>Compression, storage beyond the tank, pipelines and trucks, which DOE's production cost leaves out too.</li>
<li>Credit rules and their values, which change from year to year.</li>
<li>Whether the wind farm would have been built anyway (additionality), and where its power can be delivered (deliverability).</li>
<li>Electrochemistry, stack wear and safety engineering: devices enter only as efficiencies and load ranges.</li>
<li>Water: electrolysis consumes water too.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a16-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="bigger" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A bigger electrolyzer on the same wind farm makes each kilogram cheaper.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth, on spare wind. From 10 to 30 MW its average utilization falls from 23% to 13%, and the cost per kg rises from $3.25 to $5.65.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="claim" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If an electrolyzer's power is matched with wind over the year, its hydrogen is made without emissions.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Annual matching lets a 30 MW unit run from grid power in low-wind hours; if gas makes that power, it carries about 5.8 kg of CO₂ per kg, above DOE's 4.0 target.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="store" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Delivering wind-made hydrogen at a steady rate needs storage for weeks, not hours.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact, for this farm in 2025. A 20 MW unit's steady delivery needs at least 88 t of working storage, 59 days of its output: windy and calm seasons take turns.</p><p>That is with 44 t in the tank on 1 January and no losses; another weather year needs its own check.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a16">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="kg" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">An electrolyzer uses 57 kWh per kg. How much hydrogen does 10 MWh make?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">570 kg</li><li data-value="b">about 175 kg</li><li data-value="c">about 17.5 kg</li><li data-value="d">5.7 kg</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 175 kg: 10,000 kWh ÷ 57 kWh per kg = 175.4. 570 multiplies instead of dividing; 17.5 kg is what 1 MWh makes; 5.7 divides 57 by 10.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<li>DOE Loan Programs Office (2022). <a href="https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2022-04/LPO_ACES_EA_executed_FONSI_April2022.pdf">Advanced Clean Energy Storage project, environmental assessment DOE/EA-2182</a>, §2.2 (salt caverns).</li>
<li>DOE: <a href="https://www.energy.gov/cmei/fuels/fuel-cells">Fuel Cells</a>; <a href="https://afdc.energy.gov/fuels/electricity-benefits">AFDC, electric vehicle benefits</a>; <a href="https://afdc.energy.gov/files/u/publication/hydrogen_fuel_cell_electric_vehicles.pdf">AFDC, Hydrogen Fuel Cell Electric Vehicles</a> (January 2025), p. 5; <a href="https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2022-08/energy-saver-guide-2022.pdf">Energy Saver Guide (2022)</a>, p. 16.</li>
```
